title: The Speed Dividend: What AI Is Quietly Doing to Marketing and Creative Agency Margins
linkedin:
A website brief that used to take six hours now takes two. The deliverable hasn't changed. The invoice usually hasn't either.

That's the quiet problem AI is creating inside marketing and creative agencies right now. Production work, first drafts, social variations, basic layout, transcription, has compressed hard. Strategy and client judgement haven't moved at all.

Most agencies are still running one blended hourly rate across both. Which means the hours they save on production are, by default, a gift to the client rather than margin recovered by the business that paid for the tools.

We see the saved time land in one of three places. It becomes unbilled spare capacity nobody tracks. It becomes extra scope absorbed quietly because nobody wants an awkward pricing conversation. Or, less often, it becomes real margin because the agency repriced on purpose.

Only that third option actually pays off the investment in the tools.

The fix isn't hiding the efficiency gain. It's splitting the rate card into layers, strategic hours priced as they are, production hours moved to a fixed fee per deliverable, so the agency gets paid for the asset, not for how long it happened to take that week.

Agencies in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne are all working through this at the same time. The ones who reprice deliberately over the next year will set the market. The ones still billing like it's last year will find their margin has moved without anyone deciding it should.

AI tools have quietly cut the time behind a lot of production work, first draft copy, social content variations, basic layout, research summaries. The finished work going out to clients looks the same. The hours it used to take to produce it do not.

Most agencies haven't touched their rate card to reflect that yet, which means the time saved is, by default, going to the client rather than back into the business that invested in the tools to begin with. In our experience, saved time tends to land in one of three places: it becomes capacity nobody tracks, it becomes extra scope absorbed into the same fee, or, less often, it becomes genuine margin because the business repriced deliberately.

The fix isn't to hide the efficiency gain. It's to separate the rate card into layers, keeping strategic and client-facing hours priced as they are, and moving production work toward a fixed fee per deliverable instead of an hourly rate that no longer reflects reality.
